newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Rybkin calls for calm, backs Chechen deal.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Rybkin calls for calm, backs Chechen deal.

text.p: Russia's new security chief on Sunday began trying to repair the damage caused by his explosive predecessor Alexander Lebed, saying Kremlin officials should under no circumstances squabble in public over policies.

But Ivan Rybkin also hinted that despite his reputation as a moderate he was not prepared to be walked over, reviving a suggestion he made last year that the work of Russia's "power ministries" should be much more closely coordinated.
President Boris Yeltsin on Saturday appointed Rybkin to replace Lebed as his envoy to Chechnya as well as to the post of secretary to the powerful Security Council.
Lebed was sacked on Thursday for openly disagreeing with Kremlin colleagues during his four months in power.
"Policies should be open and transparent for all to see," Rybkin, a former parliamentary speaker who turned 50 on Sunday, told Ekho Moskvy radio.
"But it is impermissible that there should be public fights between leading officials -- they should deal with their problems by the book," he said.

Yeltsin appointed Lebed to help him fend off the threat of Communist Gennady Zyuganov in the second round of presidential elections in July, but the gruff former paratroop general soon began alienating his Kremlin colleagues.

It was the last thing Yeltsin needed as he prepared for heart surgery and the ailing Russian leader had to drag himself from his sickbed to face the cameras on Thursday to sack Lebed and again on Saturday to wish Rybkin well in his new job.

Rybkin, who unlike Lebed has no open ambitions to be president, called for an overhaul of how Russia's interior, defence and security ministries were run on the grounds that more coordination between the three was needed.
At present the Security Council coordinates the activities of the three ministries but there have been rumours that Yeltsin might soon abolish it.

Rybkin suggested a special coordinator should always be present when the three ministers reported to Yeltsin and said a new body should be set up to control all the weapons and equipment used by the three ministries' forces.
Rybkin said the idea enjoyed widespread support but his words looked more like the act of a man sending a signal that he wished to be taken seriously.
In any case, it seemed highly unlikely that the three ministries, who jealously guard the right to operate their own armed forces, would agree to give up control of their weapons.
Rybkin's appointment on Saturday followed a week of high drama in Moscow, in which Lebed was accused of plotting a creeping coup to take power from the ailing president by force.

On Sunday Rybkin, scorned by Lebed as an incompetent bureaucrat, won cautious approval from the Chechen separatists, who had previously seen Lebed as the only hope for a permanent end to 21 months of bitter fighting over the southern region.
"Blood is still leaking from this wound to the Russian state, which must be healed by everyone pulling together," Rybkin told Ekho Moskvy.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin has also vowed an August peace deal will not be scrapped and said the Security Council would continue to deal with the affair, words which found favour with rebel spokesman Movladi Udugov in the capital Grozny.

"As far as this can influence events, it's hard to say 100 percent, but in general the statements of Chernomyrdin and Rybkin that the Security Council will be pre-eminent in this question give us hope. We'll see," he told reporters.
